title: Abnormal Bleeding / Coagulopathy Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for abnormal bleeding and coagulopathy in adults, covering inherited and acquired bleeding disorders with a systematic investigation strategy based on clinical presentation and initial laboratory findings.
source_description: Hayward CPM. How I investigate for bleeding disorders. Int J Lab Hematol. 2018;40(Suppl 1):6-14.

diagnoses.name: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
key_features: Simultaneous bleeding and thrombosis
Associated with sepsis, malignancy, obstetric emergencies, or trauma
Consumption of platelets and coagulation factors
Elevated D-dimer and fibrin degradation products
Prolonged PT and aPTT with low fibrinogen

diagnoses.name: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD)
key_features: Most common inherited bleeding disorder
Mucocutaneous bleeding: epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Excessive bleeding after dental procedures or surgery
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (most types)
red_flags: Postpartum hemorrhage as VWF levels decline after delivery
Type 3 VWD with severe bleeding and undetectable VWF
recommended_tests: VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor or GP1b-binding assay)
Blood type (type O associated with lower VWF levels)

diagnoses.name: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII Deficiency)
key_features: X-linked recessive inheritance
Deep tissue bleeding: hemarthrosis, muscle hematomas
Prolonged aPTT with normal PT
Severity correlates with factor VIII activity level
Excessive bleeding after trauma or surgery

diagnoses.name: Hemophilia B (Factor IX Deficiency)
key_features: X-linked recessive inheritance
Clinical presentation similar to hemophilia A
Prolonged aPTT with normal PT
Deep tissue and joint bleeding
Less common than hemophilia A (approximately 1:5 ratio)
red_flags: Anaphylaxis to factor IX concentrates (rare but life-threatening)

diagnoses.name: Acquired Hemophilia A
key_features: Spontaneous autoantibodies against factor VIII
No prior personal or family bleeding history
Extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage and ecchymoses
Prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing study (time-dependent)
Associated with autoimmune disease, malignancy, pregnancy, or idiopathic
red_flags: Seventy-seven percent present with spontaneous bleeding
Seventy percent present with serious bleeding
Elderly patient with new-onset severe bleeding
recommended_tests: aPTT with mixing study (incubated at 37C shows incomplete correction)
Factor VIII activity level (often less than 1%)
Screen for underlying malignancy or autoimmune disease

diagnoses.name: Platelet Function Disorders
key_features: Mucocutaneous bleeding pattern
Easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia
Normal platelet count with abnormal function
May be inherited (Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier, storage pool disorders) or acquired (medications, uremia)
red_flags: Severe postsurgical or posttraumatic bleeding as first presentation
Concurrent antiplatelet medication use masking underlying disorder
recommended_tests: Whole mount electron microscopy for dense granule deficiency
Flow cytometry for surface glycoprotein assessment

diagnoses.name: Medication-Induced Bleeding
key_features: Temporal correlation with anticoagulant or antiplatelet initiation
Anticoagulants: warfarin, DOACs, heparin
Antiplatelet agents: aspirin, clopidogrel, prasugrel
NSAIDs impairing platelet function
Herbal supplements with anticoagulant properties
recommended_tests: Anti-Xa level for DOAC or heparin monitoring

diagnoses.name: Liver Disease Coagulopathy
key_features: Rebalanced hemostasis with concurrent bleeding and thrombosis risk
Prolonged PT/INR and aPTT
Low fibrinogen in advanced disease
Thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration
Variceal bleeding, mucosal bleeding

diagnoses.name: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
key_features: Paradoxical thrombosis more common than bleeding
Platelet count drop greater than 50% from baseline
Onset typically 5-10 days after heparin exposure
Can cause skin necrosis at injection sites
Thrombocytopenia may contribute to bleeding risk
red_flags: Skin necrosis at heparin injection sites

diagnoses.name: Vitamin K Deficiency
key_features: Prolonged PT with normal or mildly prolonged aPTT
Associated with malnutrition, malabsorption, prolonged antibiotic use
Corrects with vitamin K administration
Factors II, VII, IX, X affected (vitamin K-dependent)
red_flags: GI bleeding in patients with malabsorption
recommended_tests: Mixing study (PT corrects, suggesting factor deficiency)
Individual factor levels (II, VII, IX, X) if needed

diagnoses.name: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
key_features: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes
Severe thrombocytopenia
Neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures, focal deficits)
Renal impairment
ADAMTS13 activity severely deficient (less than 10%)
red_flags: Severe anemia with schistocytes on smear

diagnoses.name: Fibrinogen Disorders (Dysfibrinogenemia and Hypofibrinogenemia)
key_features: Prolonged thrombin time is characteristic finding
Can present with bleeding or paradoxically with thrombosis
Discrepancy between functional and antigenic fibrinogen levels in dysfibrinogenemia
May be congenital or acquired (liver disease)
red_flags: Fibrinogen less than 100 mg/dL with active bleeding

diagnoses.name: Factor XI Deficiency
key_features: Autosomal inheritance pattern
Variable bleeding phenotype poorly correlating with factor level
Bleeding primarily with surgery or trauma, especially mucosal surfaces
More prevalent in Ashkenazi Jewish population
Prolonged aPTT with normal PT
red_flags: Unexpected surgical bleeding despite mild aPTT prolongation

also_consider.name: Factor XIII Deficiency
also_consider.rationale: Rare but life-threatening; normal PT and aPTT with severe bleeding including umbilical stump bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage; requires specific factor XIII assay

also_consider.name: Alpha-2 Antiplasmin Deficiency
also_consider.rationale: Causes hyperfibrinolysis with delayed bleeding after initial hemostasis; not detected by standard coagulation tests; requires specific alpha-2 antiplasmin activity assay

also_consider.name: Plasminogen Activator Inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) Deficiency
also_consider.rationale: Rare cause of hyperfibrinolytic bleeding; delayed surgical or trauma-related bleeding; requires specialized fibrinolytic assays

also_consider.name: Acquired Von Willebrand Disease
also_consider.rationale: Associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, aortic stenosis, or ventricular assist devices; mimics inherited VWD but with late onset and no family history

also_consider.name: Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Vascular Type)
also_consider.rationale: Connective tissue disorder causing arterial dissection and organ rupture; easy bruising and thin translucent skin; standard coagulation tests normal

also_consider.name: Scurvy (Vitamin C Deficiency)
also_consider.rationale: Perifollicular hemorrhage, gingival bleeding, and easy bruising; consider in malnourished or elderly patients; coagulation tests normal

also_consider.name: Amyloidosis-Associated Bleeding
also_consider.rationale: Acquired factor X deficiency and vascular fragility; periorbital purpura (raccoon eyes) is pathognomonic; consider in patients with unexplained coagulopathy

also_consider.name: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
also_consider.rationale: Severe systemic inflammatory syndrome with coagulopathy, cytopenias, and organ dysfunction; high ferritin and soluble IL-2 receptor are diagnostic clues

also_consider.name: Bleeding Disorder of Unknown Cause (BDUC)
also_consider.rationale: Diagnosed when all routine hemostasis tests are normal despite significant bleeding history; may require non-routine testing for thrombomodulin-associated coagulopathy or hyperfibrinolysis

also_consider.name: Glanzmann Thrombasthenia
also_consider.rationale: Rare autosomal recessive platelet disorder with absent GPIIb/IIIa; severe mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet count; requires flow cytometry for diagnosis

also_consider.name: Bernard-Soulier Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Autosomal recessive platelet disorder with absent GPIb-IX-V complex; large platelets on blood smear; absent ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination

also_consider.name: Lupus Anticoagulant with Hypoprothrombinemia
also_consider.rationale: Paradoxical bleeding despite prolonged aPTT; associated with antiphospholipid antibodies and acquired factor II deficiency; more common in pediatric SLE

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. Approach bleeding evaluation systematically: determine whether bleeding is mucocutaneous (suggesting platelet or VWF disorder) versus deep tissue/joint (suggesting coagulation factor deficiency). Always obtain a thorough bleeding history including family history, medication review, and use of a validated bleeding assessment tool. Consider acquired causes in patients with no prior bleeding history, and test simultaneously for VWD, platelet function disorders, and coagulation defects to minimize diagnostic delay. A normal PT and aPTT do not exclude a bleeding disorder -- factor XIII deficiency, mild VWD, platelet function disorders, and hyperfibrinolytic states may all present with normal routine coagulation tests.
